---
title: "JMS: Bald God of Diplomatic Sci-Fi"
author: "Jon Minton"
date: "2026-08-22"
categories: [television, sci-fi, stories, diplomacy, myth]
draft: true

---

As discussed [previously](../../guano-guild-origin/index.qmd), one of [my father](../../book-of-nigel/index.qmd)'s favourite TV shows in the 2000s was Carnivàle, a Gothic high fantasy nominally about a circus troupe, but really about a high-stakes Manichean conflict between a sartorially elegant Dark Priest and a scruffy and reluctant Healer. I say *one of*, because I can't verify this was his favourite show of this decade, even though, being cancelled after just two seasons which promised but never quite revealed the show's deep lore and cosmic mythos, it was almost certainly his most missed show. 

When it comes to the 1990s, there's much less doubt as to his favourite TV series. 

It was Babylon 5, a sci-fi show, created by J Michael Straczynski, set on a cylindrical spinning space station which functions as something like a cross between a model UN and a cosmopolitan city. 

In the title I described the show as 'Diplomatic Sci-Fi', as surfacing and resolving conflict between alien factions through skilled negotiation and compromise forms much of the narrative backbone of the show. 

Negotiation and compromise between whom? Well, Babylon 5 focused mainly on four factions (including humans), each of which is represented by one character playing a leader/ambassador and (mostly) one character playing their aide. This is shown in @fig-faction-hierarchies. 

```{dot}
//| label: fig-faction-hierarchies
//| fig-cap: "The internal hierarchies of Babylon 5's four peer factions, as established in the early seasons. Each delegation pairs an ambassador with an aide; the human hosts instead field a command triad, with two subordinates at rough parity."
graph b5_dyads {
  graph [newrank=true, splines=true, nodesep=0.45, ranksep=1.1,
         fontname="Helvetica", bgcolor="transparent"]
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="white",

  edge [color="gray45"]

  subgraph cluster_humans {

    ivanova   [label="Ivanova\nFirst Officer"]
```

So, for the most part, this is a symmetrical structure of senior-junior structures operating in parallel across four (initially, broadly) equal groups. 

JMS was a prolific scriptwriter by the time Babylon 5 was ideated, commissioned, and written, and this (broadly) 4-by-2 structure for the central characters is surely no accident. Instead, it's a *mechanism for scenes and dialogue*. How so? Because it creates a *lot* of dyads: ways of placing characters together which have distinct dynamics, similarities, differences, and scopes for both commonality and conflict. As discussed in [my post on Frasier](../new-frasiers-eerie-familiarity/index.qmd), the number of distinct dyads can be worked out using combinatorial mathematics. If we're looking at 9 principal characters, and just considering scenes involving any two of them, then the number of two-hander scenes that emerges is $C(9, 2) = \frac{9!}{2!(9-2)!} = \frac{9 \times 8}{2} = 36$.

With 36 basic dyads involving principal characters alone, as well as frequent additional guest stars and secondary characters, this is beyond the realm of a typical basic character study or sitcom (maybe 3-5 characters), and instead is in the deep ensemble territory of a soap opera (albeit, set in space. So, a Space Opera?). 

Indeed, strip away the (now endearingly retro) CGI space scenes and the reference to very high off-screen stakes (10,000 troops here, a planet there), and focus instead on some of the slightly am-dram costuming, the shaky sets, the cobbled-together props, the 20+ episodes per year, and Babylon 5 probably really is, ultimately, at least at the level of scenes, a soap opera.[^ref-jon-sso]

[^ref-jon-sso]: I've written before about [the concealed genre of 'the sweary soap opera'](../on-sweary-soaps/index.qmd). Babylon 5 is strictly PG-rated in terms of language, but the power fantasies inherent in the plot operate, I'd suggest, similarly to that of 'bad language' in SSOs: to conceal the genre and give licence to, primarily, male viewers to enjoy watching a soap opera.
